title-group.article-title: Intensification and Low-Carbon Performance: A Two-Stage Framework for Evaluating Urban Construction Land Use Efficiency Across 268 Chinese Cities

abstract.p: Evaluating urban construction land use efficiency (UCLUE) from the dual perspectives of intensification and low-carbon performance is critical for sustainable urban development. Previous studies often assess this efficiency from a single perspective, failing to capture potential conflicts and synergies between economic density and emission reduction goals. This study adopts a two-stage super-SBM approach to evaluate UCLUE of 268 Chinese cities from 2001 to 2021, systematically examining both intensification and low-carbon dimensions. Results show that (1) the average efficiency from an intensification perspective remains relatively low and exhibits a fluctuating pattern of initial increase, subsequent decline, and final rebound, with the eastern region ranking highest, followed by the western and central regions. (2) The low-carbon efficiency follows a U-shaped trajectory over the study period, with the eastern region again performing best, followed by the western and central regions. (3) Many cities exhibit relatively low efficiency in both dimensions, with 146 of the 268 cities (54.48%) falling into the Low–Low development mode and only 53 cities (19.78%) achieving the High–High development mode. Furthermore, cities with larger population sizes demonstrate stronger sustainable performance. These findings provide empirical evidence for identifying spatial heterogeneities and formulating differentiated, context-specific land use policies to coordinate urban expansion and carbon reduction.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: As the world’s largest developing country, China has achieved remarkable urbanization progress since its reform and opening-up. According to data from the National Bureau of Statistics, China’s urbanization rate rose from 17.92% in 1978 to 64.72% in 2021, while urban construction land (UCL) expanded from 6720 km2 to 59,451.69 km2 during 1981–2022, growing at an average annual rate of 5.46%. While this rapid UCL expansion has contributed significantly to economic development, it has also led to considerable inefficiencies in land use and triggered negative externalities such as regional incoordination, intensified land pressure, and resource wastage [1]. Furthermore, these issues have exacerbated environmental degradation, ecological imbalances, and human–land conflicts, thereby threatening urban sustainable development. According to the White Paper on the Revitalization and Upgrading of Inefficient Land Use and Assets, the total area of inefficient UCL now exceeds 4000 km2, which is larger than three times the built-up area of Shanghai. In 2024, the average vacancy rate of industrial plants in China exceeded 30%, and even core areas of central cities could not escape the trend of continuously rising vacancy rates. UCL serves as the spatial foundation for integrated production-living-ecological functions within urban systems [2]. Therefore, enhancing its utilization efficiency is not only vital for addressing land resource supply-demand imbalances but also essential for overcoming resource-environmental constraints and advancing high-quality urban development. In response to these challenges, the Chinese government has prioritized improving the urban construction land use efficiency (UCLUE) through policies aimed at fostering intensive land management. As mandated by the National Land Planning Outline (2016–2030), key measures include implementing dual controls on UCL total area and utilization intensity, enforcing stringent UCL access standards, innovating land-conservation models, and promoting land-efficient technologies. The outline further emphasizes strict limitations on new allocations of UCL and effective management to curb disorderly urban expansion. Additionally, the report from the 20th National Congress of the Communist Party of China advocates for the implementation of a comprehensive conservation strategy and the promotion of resource-efficient utilization across all sectors. Therefore, enhancing the UCLUE with a focus on intensive development is crucial.

Furthermore, UCL constitutes the spatial foundation for urban socioeconomic activities, which account for approximately 75% of global carbon emissions [3]. Wang et al. [4] suggested that with the continuous expansion of UCL, China’s energy consumption has been increasing. Carbon emissions have risen from 0.41 billion tons in 2001 to 12.6 billion tons in 2023. Since 2005, China has overtaken the United States to become the world’s largest carbon emitter [5]. The Chinese government has committed to achieving “Dual Carbon Targets”, reaching peak carbon emissions by 2030 and attaining carbon neutrality by 2060. This commitment reflects both China’s international responsibilities as a major power and domestic imperatives for sustainable modernization. Consequently, enhancing UCLUE under carbon constraints has emerged as an urgent priority [6]. The Action Plan for Carbon Dioxide Peaking Before 2030 explicitly mandates a low-carbon transformation in urban-rural development, promotes clustered urban growth patterns, calls for the scientific determination of construction scales, and controls new UCL expansion. Therefore, transitioning UCL utilization from extensive high-emission models to intensive low-carbon approaches now constitutes a fundamental strategy within China’s land management framework. Evaluating UCLUE under the dual constraints of intensification and decarbonization is thus critical for achieving China’s long-term strategic goals of low-carbon economic transformation and sustainable development.

The conceptualization of UCLUE arises from the ongoing scholarly discourse surrounding the measurement of land use efficiency, with the current literature diverging into three predominant definitional frameworks. The prevailing perspective equates UCLUE with economic output per unit of land [7], utilizing singular metrics such as the ratio of secondary and tertiary industry output to land area [8] or GDP per urban land area [9]. Alternatively, some scholars define UCLUE as a measure of land resource productivity and sustainability, which is often measured through ratios reflecting urban expansion relative to population growth [10]. For instance, Koroso et al. [11] conducted a quantitative analysis of UCLUE across 16 Ethiopian cities by comparing the rates of spatial land expansion with those of population growth. An emerging perspective frames land utilization as an integrated input–output system that emphasizes socioeconomic–ecological synergies [12], wherein UCLUE represents the capacity to balance social, economic, and environmental outcomes [13]. This includes input–output ratios that incorporate land, capital, and labor against multidimensional outputs, as well as the optimization of economic growth alongside environmental benefits while minimizing resource consumption [14]. Collectively, these UCLUE definitions reveal a conceptual bifurcation between narrow interpretations emphasizing economic efficiency and population density versus broader frameworks encompassing social–economic–environmental dimensions—an evolution that mirrors the methodological transition from singular metrics to composite assessment systems [15,16]. Recent scholarship advocates for treating UCLUE as a complex multi-input/multi-output production system in order to avoid the limitations of single indicators [17], proposing a comprehensive input–output evaluation framework for holistic assessments of UCLUE [18,19].

With the advancement of land intensification and low-carbon development paradigms, scholarly evaluations of UCLUE have evolved through dual analytical lenses. From the intensification perspective, researchers quantify UCLUE using development intensity measurement models and systems of indicators for intensive land utilization [20,21]. For example, Peng et al. [22] established a multidimensional framework that incorporates metrics on land input intensity, utilization intensity, utilization efficiency, and utilization structure to measure UCLUE. Under carbon emission constraints, research on evaluating UCLUE has integrated carbon indicators as undesirable outputs within the efficiency evaluation framework [23]. This paradigm is exemplified in the works of Su et al. [24] and Wu et al. [6], who incorporated carbon emissions as undesirable environmental outputs to develop a comprehensive UCLUE evaluation indicator system. As low-carbon intensification emerges as a new direction for land regulation in China, some scholars have investigated the nexus between land intensification and low-carbon development [25]. For example, Wang et al. [26] took the Wuhan Economic Development Zone as the study area to demonstrate how intensive urban land utilization contributes to achieving low-carbon objectives. Xie et al. [27] employed an industrial land intensification metric (energy consumption per unit area) at the provincial level in China to quantify its impact on carbon emissions.

These research findings have provided theoretical foundations for promoting the low-carbon and intensive development of urban construction land use (UCLU). However, several limitations persist within the current literature. First, most existing studies assess UCLUE solely from either carbon emissions or intensification perspectives, lacking an integrated assessment framework that synthesizes both low-carbon and intensive land-use objectives. While a limited number of studies have attempted to combine indicators of carbon emission with those of land use intensification, it is important to note that the low-carbon transition of UCL cannot be simplistically equated with mere carbon reduction. This transition requires a comprehensive consideration of multifaceted factors, including industrial structure optimization, energy mix adjustment, technological advancement, population quality enhancement, and carbon sink improvement [28]. Second, evaluating UCLUE cannot be reduced to a mechanical aggregation of intensification and low-carbon objectives, as the relationship between intensification and decarbonization is complex and non-linear. On one hand, enhanced intensive use of UCL typically implies greater utilization intensity per unit area, which often correlates with diminished carbon sinks and increased reliance on carbon-intensive energy inputs, thereby elevating overall emissions [29]. On the other hand, intensified UCL can lead to improved energy efficiency per unit and reduce the demand for land expansion, ultimately curbing carbon emissions [30]. Third, nationwide city-scale studies evaluating UCLUE remain scarce. The significant variations in natural endowments and socioeconomic development across cities complicate the extrapolation of insights from regional-level analyses to urban-scale UCLUE disparities.

This study makes two primary contributions to the existing literature. First, it develops an integrated assessment framework that synthesizes both intensification and low-carbon objectives for evaluating UCLUE. Moving beyond previous studies that narrowly equate low-carbon transition with mere carbon reduction, this framework conceptualizes low-carbon development as a comprehensive system encompassing multiple connotations. Second, by applying this dual perspective framework to a large scale panel of 268 Chinese cities during 2001–2021, the study systematically reveals the spatiotemporal evolution and regional disparities of land use performance. Through categorizing urban development into four distinct modes, this nationwide analysis identifies combinations of relative efficiency levels in the two dimensions across different urban contexts and population sizes, providing empirical evidence for formulating differentiated spatial planning policies.

To achieve these objectives, three primary tasks are undertaken. First, an integrated evaluation index system is established, incorporating comprehensive indicators for both land use intensification and multidimensional low-carbon development. Second, a two-stage super-SBM model is employed to measure UCLUE across 268 Chinese cities from 2001 to 2021. Third, the study examines the spatiotemporal patterns and classifies development modes of these dual efficiencies to derive specific policy recommendations for transitioning from extensive expansion to sustainable development pathways. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 details the data and methodology. Section 3 presents the empirical findings. Section 4 discusses the empirical findings. Section 5 summarizes key conclusions.

sec.title: 2.1. Conceptualizing a Two-Stage Evolution in UCLU
sec.p: UCL has been a fundamental driver of China’s economic growth and population agglomeration since the Reform and Opening-up. Given land scarcity and initially extensive utilization patterns, the primary objective during this early phase was to achieve intensive land use [26]. This focus aligns with Rostow’s theory of economic growth stages, where initial industrialization prioritizes factor accumulation and efficiency gains through capital and land-intensive strategies. Similarly, land rent theory supports high-density and high-intensity development as a means to maximize economic returns and agglomerate capital, labor, and technology. Consequently, early-stage UCL in China was characterized by rapid scale expansion and a “high-input, high-output” model, with intensive land-use efficiency serving as the primary performance indicator [31]. Environmental externalities, including carbon emissions, were not yet a binding constraint on development priorities at this stage.

As China’s urbanization entered a phase emphasizing high-quality development, the environmental repercussions of a purely economic-intensive UCL model—characterized by high energy consumption and emissions—became increasingly apparent, threatening long-term sustainability [32,33]. Guided by the theory of sustainable development, which calls for harmonizing economic, social, and environmental objectives, UCL governance has initiated a strategic transition toward low-carbon development. The core focus consequently shifted from quantitative expansion to qualitative enhancement, pursued through technological upgrading, structural optimization, and ecological integration. This shift reflects a broader evaluation framework where cities began to assess UCL performance not only by its economic and social outputs but also by its ecological and environmental benefits. Importantly, this low-carbon transition does not negate the principle of intensification; rather, it integrates carbon reduction into the foundational goal of efficient land use, thereby promoting a transformed model characterized by lower pollution, lower emissions, and higher efficiency.

In summary, the evolution of UCLU can be conceptualized as a dynamic, two-stage process: an intensive development stage and a low-carbon development stage. The intensive stage emphasizes maximizing output per unit of land area and establishing a foundation for subsequent development. The low-carbon stage represents a deepening and expansion of the foundation established in the intensive stage, explicitly incorporating goals to reduce carbon emissions and minimize environmental impacts [34]. It seeks to sustain the economic and social benefits of intensive land use while improving environmental performance, thereby promoting coordinated social, ecological, and economic progress. This two-stage conceptualization of UCLU provides the theoretical basis for evaluating UCLUE from the intensification and low-carbon perspectives, as illustrated in Figure 1.

sec.title: 2.2. Two-Stage Super-SBM Model for Measuring UCLUE
sec.p: Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) has been widely employed in measuring UCLUE due to its ability to evaluate relative efficiency in multi-input and multi-output systems without requiring a predefined production function [15,35]. However, traditional DEA models exhibit several limitations. First, they treat each decision-making unit (DMU) as a “black box”, overlooking the internal structure and intermediate processes linking inputs to outputs, which may lead to an overestimation of efficiency. Second, efficiency scores are constrained to the range [0, 1], often resulting in multiple DMUs being equally efficient and thus incomparable [36]. Third, conventional models typically neglect undesirable outputs, leading to biased assessments that deviate from actual production activities. To address these shortcomings, Färe and Grosskopf [37] proposed the network DEA model, which decomposes the single-stage production process into multiple serial substages. By treating the output of one stage as the input to the next, this approach effectively connects adjacent stages of the system, enhances transparency, and allows for stage-specific efficiency evaluation. Concurrently, Tone [36] developed the super-slacks-based measure (super-SBM) model, which incorporates undesirable outputs and permits efficiency scores to exceed 1, thereby overcoming the ranking limitations of traditional DEA. Building on this method, this study adopts a two-stage assessment framework to separately estimate stage-specific efficiencies.

As the analysis of Section 2.1, UCL development involves complex, multi-stage processes characterized by multiple inputs and outputs. Therefore, this study adopts a two-stage super-SBM approach to evaluate UCLUE from two complementary perspectives: intensification and low-carbon performance. In the first stage, a standard super-SBM model is applied to assess UCLUE from the intensification perspective (UCLUE-IN). The second stage employs a super-SBM model that accounts for undesirable outputs to evaluate UCLUE from a low-carbon perspective (UCLUE-LC), with the outputs of the first stage serving as inputs to the second. Both stages are specified under the variable returns-to-scale (VRS) assumption, with the efficiency frontier separately constructed and independently solved using pooled observations from 268 cities over the period 2001–2021. This two-stage framework enables a more nuanced understanding of the efficiency of each stage in the UCL development process and supports more targeted policy implications.

Since the two efficiency scores reflect performance relative to their respective frontiers rather than stage-to-stage conversion rates, a higher UCLUE-IN does not necessarily correspond to a higher UCLUE-LC, and the two scores should not be directly compared as measures of the same performance.

sec.title: 2.3. Selection of Input–Output Indicators
sec.p: Applying the two-stage super-SBM model requires constructing a coherent input–output indicator system based on the principles of scientific relevance and data availability.

For measuring UCLUE-IN (Stage 1), this study selects land, capital and labor as input indicators. Land input is represented by per capita urban construction land area, as it is the fundamental spatial carrier for all urban economic activities. Capital input is measured by fixed asset investment per unit of UCL area, reflecting the capital intensity invested to generate returns from land. Labor input is denoted by the number of employees in secondary and tertiary industries per unit land area, capturing the human resource factor driving economic output. The output of this stage mainly involves economic and social benefits. Economic benefit is measured by the added value of secondary and tertiary industries, which constitutes the primary economic output generated from UCL. Social benefit is represented by two indicators: per capita road area, reflecting the level of intensive infrastructure development; and urbanization rate (proportion of urban resident population to total population), representing the socio-demographic outcome of land use intensification.

For measuring UCLUE-LC (Stage 2), the outputs from Stage 1 serve as the inputs. These indicators describe the economic and social conditions that cities build on in pursuing low-carbon development. The outputs of this stage are multi-dimensional, selected to capture key drivers and outcomes of low-carbon UCLU from six aspects: (1) population quality: number of university students per 10,000 inhabitants, indicating the human capital base for adopting low-carbon technologies and lifestyles. (2) Industrial structure: proportion of tertiary industry added value to GDP, as a more service-oriented structure typically correlates with lower carbon intensity. (3) Energy structure: ratio of non-coal consumption to total energy consumption, reflecting the progress in decarbonizing the energy consumption. (4) Technological level: number of patent applications, indicating general innovation capacity that may support energy-efficiency improvements and low-carbon technological upgrading. (5) Urban green level: urban green space area, reflecting green-space provision that can contribute to low-carbon UCLU by enhancing vegetation carbon sequestration and cooling-related energy consumption. (6) Carbon emissions: carbon emissions from UCL are included as an undesirable output, acknowledging the negative environmental externality of land use [38].
In summary, the two-stage UCLUE evaluation index system is constructed as presented in Table 1.

sec.title: 2.4. Data Source and Processing
sec.p: This study utilizes panel data spanning 268 prefecture-level cities in China from 2001 to 2021. Data on urban land area—including UCL area, per capita road area, and urban greening area—were sourced from the China Urban Construction Statistical Yearbook. Socioeconomic data, encompassing population, labor force, GDP, fixed asset investment, and industrial added value, were obtained from the China City Statistical Yearbook, supplemented by relevant provincial and municipal statistical yearbooks and bulletins. Data on patent applications were collected from the National Intellectual Property Administration. Missing values were imputed using linear interpolation. Price adjustments were based on provincial fixed-asset investment price indices and municipal value-added indices for the secondary and tertiary sectors, respectively.

To account for the price effect, total fixed asset investment and the added value of the secondary and tertiary industries were converted to constant prices for the year 2000 using the fixed asset investment price index and the industrial added value index, respectively. Due to the lack of city-level energy consumption data, this study estimates the energy consumption associated with each city’s UCL by using an indirect method based on the ratio of municipal GDP to provincial GDP, following the approach of Liu et al. [46]. In alignment with the research of Zhang et al. [47], nine energy sources were considered in the calculation: coal, coke, crude oil, fuel oil, gasoline, kerosene, diesel, natural gas, and electricity. The calculation of carbon emissions (C) is performed as C=∑Ei×SCFi×CEFi. The provincial energy consumption data (Ei) and the standard coal conversion coefficient (SCFi) were obtained from the China Energy Statistical Yearbook, while the carbon emission factors (CEFi) were collected from the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories.

sec.title: 3.1.1. Analysis of the Temporal Evolution of UCLUE-IN
sec.p: Based on the super-SBM model, the UCLUE-IN of 268 Chinese cities from 2001 to 2021 is calculated, and the annual average trend is presented in Figure 2. The overall average efficiency was low at 0.142, exhibiting a distinct pattern of an initial increase, followed by a decline and a subsequent rebound. With all other settings unchanged, the conventional SBM estimates yielded nearly identical efficiency rankings (Spearman’s ρ = 0.999), supporting the robustness of these rankings to model choice.

From 2001 to 2006, UCLUE-IN showed an upward trend, rising from 0.107 to 0.147. During this period, China’s accession to the WTO accelerated industrialization and urbanization, with the urbanization rate rising from 37.66% to 44.34% and UCL area expanding by approximately 41.23%. Accelerated infrastructure construction and intensified UCL development contributed to the improvement in UCLUE-IN. Furthermore, the State Council’s Decision on Deepening Reform and Strictly Managing Land emphasized strict control over new UCL scale and revitalization of existing land, providing institutional support for intensive use of UCL.

The period between 2006 and 2014 witnessed a slight decline in UCLUE-IN. This decline can be attributed to the rapid proliferation of urban development zones, which often led to inefficient and disorderly land expansion [24]. Moreover, the 2008 global financial crisis suppressed export trade and urban economic growth, further reducing resource utilization efficiency [17].

From 2014 to 2021, UCLUE-IN rebounded rapidly, rising from 0.133 to 0.210. This improvement was mainly driven by policy optimization and the advancement of new urbanization. In 2014, the Ministry of Land and Resources issued the Guiding Opinions on Promoting the Saving and Intensive Use of Land, and the State Council released the National New Urbanization Plan (2014–2020). These policies required local governments to implement strict farmland protection and intensive land-use systems, optimize land-use structure, and further promote land conservation and intensive management.

Regionally, the eastern region consistently recorded the highest UCLUE-IN, exceeding the national average. The central and western regions exhibited a shifting pattern: before 2013, the central region outperformed the western region, but this relationship reversed thereafter. In 2021, the UCLUE-IN values were ranked as follows: eastern region (0.309) > western region (0.177) > central region (0.132), suggesting a positive correlation between UCLUE-IN and regional economic development level [48]. Although both central and western regions showed upward trends, their efficiency remained below the national average, highlighting the need for continued efforts to promote intensive land use.

sec.title: 3.1.2. Analysis of the Spatial Evolution of UCLUE-IN
sec.p: Following Dong et al. [18], the natural breaks method in ArcGIS 10.8.1 was applied to classify UCLUE-IN values into four levels: low efficiency (UCLUE-IN < 0.126), medium efficiency (0.126 ≤ UCLUE-IN < 0.318), medium-high efficiency (0.318 ≤ UCLUE-IN < 0.701), high efficiency (UCLUE-IN ≥ 0.701). Figure 3 illustrates the spatial distribution pattern of these categories from 2001 to 2021.

In 2001, nearly 200 cities, accounting for 74% of the sample, fell into the low-efficiency category, exhibiting a spatially concentrated distribution. Only 10 cities, representing less than 4%, belonged to the medium-high and above categories (UCLUE-IN ≥ 0.318), and these were predominantly located in the eastern region. By 2021, the proportion of low-efficiency cities dropped below 50%, while cities in the medium-high and above categories increased to 18%. This trend indicates notable progress in the intensive utilization of UCL across Chinese cities.

Spatially, UCLUE-IN displayed a distinct pattern characterized by higher efficiency in the east and lower efficiency in the west. High-efficiency clusters were mainly concentrated in the eastern region, where these cities benefited from population agglomeration and developmental advantages that enhance input–output efficiency [13]. In contrast, low-efficiency areas were widespread across central and western China, where they were constrained by weaker economic foundations and limited technological capacity. Notably, nearly 80% of the cities remained at relatively low efficiency levels throughout the study period, underscoring the urgent need for regionally differentiated policies to optimize factor input and improve intensive land use.

sec.title: 3.2.1. Analysis of the Temporal Evolution of UCLUE-LC
sec.p: As shown in Figure 4, the temporal trend of UCLUE-LC followed a pronounced U-shaped curve, declining from 0.138 in 2001 to 0.097 in 2004 before rising overall to 0.392 in 2021. The corresponding conventional SBM check likewise showed highly consistent efficiency rankings (Spearman’s ρ = 0.998), supporting the robustness of UCLUE-LC rankings.

During the period from 2001 to 2004, UCLUE-LC fluctuated and declined from 0.138 to 0.097, which reflected the high-energy, high-emission characteristics of early urban expansion. This decline was mainly driven by China’s industrial structure, which was dominated by heavy industry, and its continued dependence on fossil fuels. According to data from the National Bureau of Statistics, from 2001 to 2004, the proportion of secondary industry exceeded 45%, with heavy industry accounting for over 60%, and coal dominated energy consumption (accounting for over 68%). To some extent, these factors constrained the low-carbon development of UCL.

From 2004 to 2020, UCLUE-LC increased steadily, reaching 0.399 by 2020. This improvement was driven by national energy-saving and emission-reduction targets introduced since the 11th Five-Year Plan, along with a series of low-carbon policies. For example, the Comprehensive Work Plan for Energy Conservation and Emission Reduction during the 13th Five-Year Plan Period reinforced carbon intensity control targets. Concurrently, industrial and energy structures were optimized, energy efficiency improved, and low-carbon pilot programs were implemented [18]. Improvements in educational attainment and the influx of skilled talents further supported green technological innovation and urban governance efficiency [49].

Regionally, all three major regions followed a similar pattern of decline followed by rise, consistent with the national average (Figure 4). In 2001, the eastern region initially lagged behind the western region but surpassed it after 2004, maintaining the highest UCLUE-LC values thereafter. This shift can be attributed to the eastern region’s advantages in capital, policy, and early progress in coordinating economic growth with environmental protection [50]. The central and western regions showed a crossover pattern: after 2012, the western region exceeded the central region, a trend that can be partly explained by the deeper integration of green development concepts into urbanization and ecological construction [24]. By 2021, the ranking was as follows: eastern region (0.423) > western region (0.390) > central region (0.360), indicating that improving UCLUE-LC in central cities remains a critical challenge.

sec.title: 3.2.2. Analysis of the Spatial Evolution of UCLUE-LC
sec.p: Similar to Section 3.1.2, UCLUE-LC values were classified into four levels using the natural breaks method: low efficiency (UCLUE-LC < 0.170), medium efficiency (0.170 ≤ UCLUE-LC < 0.355), medium-high efficiency (0.355 ≤ UCLUE-LC < 0.618), and high efficiency (UCLUE-LC ≥ 0.618). Figure 5 presents the spatial evolution of these categories.

In 2001, nearly 240 cities, accounting for 89% of the sample, fell into the low-efficiency category, while only 20 cities, representing 7.5%, reached medium-high and above levels (UCLUE-LC ≥ 0.355). By 2021, low UCLUE-LC cities decreased sharply to 16 (6%), whereas medium-high and above UCLUE-LC cities increased to 116 (43%), indicating significant progress in low-carbon land use.

Spatially, high-efficiency areas evolved from dispersed patches in the east and west in 2001 to encompassing core urban agglomerations across almost all regions by 2021. This expansion was closely associated with major policy drivers: outward expansion of medium-efficiency areas in the east followed the binding targets established in the 11th Five-Year Plan on energy conservation and emission reduction, and further diffusion to central and western regions occurred after the low-carbon pilot city policy and the regional coordination strategies implemented post-2011. This evolution has given rise to an emerging spatial pattern characterized by the eastern region leading and the central and western regions developing in coordination.

sec.title: 3.3. Integrated Analysis of UCLUE-IN and UCLUE-LC
3.3.1. A Typology of Urban Development Patterns
sec.p: To categorize cities according to their performance in both intensive and low-carbon dimensions, we constructed a four-quadrant typology using their average UCLUE-IN and UCLUE-LC scores over 2001–2021 [51]. The national averages of these city-level mean scores (0.142 for UCLUE-IN and 0.221 for UCLUE-LC) served as benchmarks for distinguishing relatively high and low efficiency in each dimension. As shown in Figure 6, four distinct urban development patterns were identified: High UCLUE-IN–High UCLUE-LC (H-H), High UCLUE-IN–Low UCLUE-LC (H-L), Low UCLUE-IN–High UCLUE-LC (L-H), and Low UCLUE-IN–Low UCLUE-LC (L-L). When efficiency scores were held fixed, recalculating the mean thresholds after omitting each city reassigned at most three of the remaining 267 cities (1.12%), indicating that the classification is relatively robust to threshold changes induced by individual cities.

The H-H group, with above-average efficiency in both dimensions, comprises 53 cities. These cities are mainly distributed in the eastern coastal areas, including the Yangtze River Delta and the Pearl River Delta urban agglomerations, with a few scattered in more developed regions of central and western China, such as Nanchang and Chongqing. Among them, Shenzhen, Shanghai, and Nanjing are the top three performers. These cities successfully achieve high intensive use efficiency and strong low-carbon performance by leveraging their high economic development levels, advanced industrial technologies, and strict environmental regulations. Consequently, they serve as pioneering areas for integrated intensive and low-carbon UCL development.

The H-L group consists of 33 cities. These cities are mainly distributed in the Bohai Rim region, the North China Plain, and the Northeast heavy industry base. Among them, Shantou, Weihai, and Wuhai are representative cities. These cities have achieved intensive development of UCL through land use planning and industrial agglomeration. However, their carbon emission intensity remains at a relatively high level due to industrial structures traditionally dominated by heavy industry, a high-carbon energy consumption mix, and resource-dependent development models [19]. Consequently, their UCL development pattern can be characterized as intensive yet high-carbon.

The L-H group comprises 36 cities. These cities are mainly distributed in ecological barrier areas in the southwest and northwest, with Sanya, Lijiang, and Zhangjiajie exhibiting the largest disparities between their UCLUE-IN and UCLUE-LC scores. These cities have experienced relatively slow UCL expansion, and their industrial structures are dominated by low-energy-consuming sectors such as agriculture, ecology, and tourism. Although UCL development intensity remains low, these cities exhibit a pronounced low-carbon development orientation, resulting in a development pattern that can be described as low-carbon yet extensive.

The L-L group contains the largest number of cities, with 146 in total. These cities are widely distributed across the central and western regions of China, with Baiyin, Jincheng, and Songyuan ranking as the three lowest performers. These cities face multiple constraints, including extensive UCL expansion, industrial structure dominated by low-value-added sectors, and persistently low energy utilization efficiency. Consequently, they have failed to achieve both efficient UCL utilization and meaningful carbon emission reduction, making them priority areas for advancing the dual goals of UCL intensification and decarbonization.

sec.title: 3.3.2. Analysis of Urban Subgroups by City Size
sec.p: In accordance with the 2014 directive from the State Council, cities are classified into five categories based on their permanent resident population: small cities (<0.5 million), medium-sized cities (0.5 million ≤ population < 1 million), large cities (1 million ≤ population <5 million), huge cities (5 million ≤ population <10 million), and megacities (≥10 million). The 268 cities are classified into five categories, and the average values of UCLUE-IN and UCLUE-LC from 2001 to 2021 for each category are shown in Figure 7. As illustrated in this figure, for both UCLUE-IN and UCLUE-LC, cities across categories exhibit a consistent pattern: megacities > huge cities > large cities > medium-sized cities > small cities. Given unequal sample sizes across the five categories and unequal variances in UCLUE-IN, Welch’s ANOVA was used to compare average efficiency values, followed by Games-Howell pairwise comparisons. Welch’s ANOVA identified overall differences in both efficiency measures (both p < 0.001), although Games–Howell comparisons found no significant differences between huge cities and megacities for either measure. Jonckheere–Terpstra tests and Spearman correlations further supported an overall increasing trend across the five ordered categories (all permutation-based p values < 0.001). Thus, the overall upward pattern does not imply significant differences between every pair of adjacent categories.

Specifically, UCLUE-IN shows an overall increasing pattern across cities of different scales, with its average value rising from 0.060 in small cities to 0.629 in megacities. In contrast, while UCLUE-LC also increases with city size, its growth rate is relatively moderate. This divergence gives rise to a notable pattern in the relative performance of the two efficiency measures across city-size categories. Megacities demonstrate leading levels of both UCLUE-IN and UCLUE-LC, whereas small and medium-sized cities have lower average efficiency values. This indicates that larger city size is associated with higher efficiency in the intensive and low-carbon development of UCL.

sec.title: 4.1. Spatiotemporal Characteristics of UCLUE
sec.p: The results indicate that from 2001 to 2021, the average value of UCLUE-IN in China was relatively low, presenting a fluctuating upward trend. This finding is consistent with the research results of Zhang et al. [52]. Liu et al. [13] attributed the relatively low level of UCLUE-IN to the limited carrying capacity of UCL and its irrational expansion and allocation under existing input conditions. Consistent with the studies of Liu et al. [13], this study found that UCLUE-IN remained at the highest level in the eastern region. This can be attributed to its strategic geographical location and high-capacity infrastructure. However, there are certain differences in regional efficiency rankings between this study and previous research. In this study, the UCLUE-IN values of the regions from high to low are the eastern region, the western region, and the central region, which differs from the regional ranking of “eastern region > central region > western region” reported by Liu et al. [13]. This discrepancy may be attributed to two factors. Firstly, differences in measurement indicators and methods may have introduced systematic biases in the measurement results. Secondly, it may be due to the different research periods. This study covers a critical phase of accelerated optimization in the regional development landscape, during which the western region experienced rapid growth. Relatively low land costs and abundant natural resources have attracted investment to the western region, promoting efficient UCLU in the area [14].

Due to differences in resource endowments, the relative scarcity of production factors, and the degree of economic prosperity, there are significant regional differences in UCLUE-LC [8]. The eastern region performed best in terms of UCLUE-LC, followed by the western region, while the central region performed the worst. This is consistent with the findings of Zhou and Lu [14]. In fact, most of the developed cities are concentrated in eastern China. Rapid economic growth has promoted the development of emerging technologies, reduced resource consumption in green industries, and actively promoted the low-carbon development of UCL [19]. Zhao et al. [53] point out that urban population growth, particularly the influx of skilled talent, has injected significant impetus into the green development of cities, positioning the UCL in the eastern region favorably in terms of low-carbon development. Notably, the UCLUE-LC values measured in this study are consistently lower than those reported by Su et al. [24] and Wu et al. [6]. This discrepancy primarily stems from differences in the evaluation framework. Prior studies typically treat carbon emissions as the undesirable output within the UCLUE assessment and conduct efficiency calculations within a single stage. In contrast, this study comprehensively adopts indicators for UCL low-carbon development based on the multidimensional connotations of low-carbon development, including aspects such as population quality, industrial structure, energy structure, technological level, and urban green level. Furthermore, we decompose the UCL process into two stages—intensive land use and low-carbon development—and measure efficiency accordingly. This dual-stage, multi-dimensional evaluation approach provides a more comprehensive and accurate depiction of UCLUE-LC, with results that better reflect actual development levels.

sec.title: 4.2. Disparities in Various Development Models of UCL in China
sec.p: The spatial distribution of the four types of cities (H-H, H-L, L-H, and L-L) shows obvious regional differences. Among them, H-H group cities are mainly distributed in the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration, the Bohai Economic Zone, and other eastern coastal areas, while L-L group cities are widely distributed in the central and western regions. This is consistent with the research results of Yu et al. [54], who noted that the Yangtze River Delta and the Pearl River Delta are on the efficiency frontier during the study period, while the land resources in the Central Plains and western regions are underutilized, resulting in low UCLUE. Regarding cities with strong sustainability (the H-H group), Shenzhen, Shanghai, and Nanjing stand out as the most prominent. As China’s earliest special economic zone, Shenzhen has strictly controlled the addition of new UCL since the reform and opening up and has intensified the redevelopment of existing UCL. Meanwhile, as a low-carbon pilot city, Shenzhen has actively promoted the transformation and upgrading of industries towards high-tech and high-end services, achieving a continuous decline in carbon emissions under high-intensity development [55]. Shanghai, as a leading first-tier city in China, has promoted the intensive and low-carbon utilization of UCL through its highly concentrated economic activities and strict land use control policies [48]. Nanjing has adopted a spatial development strategy characterized by “multiple centers and cluster-style” development. Meanwhile, it has substantial scientific research and talent reserves. In 2021, the proportion of people with college degrees or above in Nanjing reached 35.7%, and the number of R&D personnel reached 181,900. These factors provide strong support for the city’s low-carbon development. Consequently, UCL intensive and low-carbon development in the H-H group has attained a mature and benchmark-level stage.

Among the cities in the H-L group, Shantou and Weihai, as coastal industrial cities, have achieved intensive UCLU through strict industrial park entry management and the evaluation mechanism based on output per unit area. Nevertheless, their core industries, such as high-end manufacturing in Shantou and equipment manufacturing in Weihai, as well as their supporting infrastructure, still mainly rely on fossil energy, resulting in dense economic activities accompanied by equally dense carbon emissions. Wuhai, following the Adjustment Plan for the Land Use Master Plan of Wuhai City (2006–2020), has advanced UCL conservation and intensification. However, as a resource-based city, Wuhai’s economic development has long relied on high-energy-consuming industries such as coal power and coal chemical industry, resulting in high carbon emission intensity.

Among the L-H group cities, Sanya, Lijiang, and Zhangjiajie are typical representative cities. All three are tourism-oriented cities that demonstrate high efficiency in UCL low-carbon development, possess a well-developed tertiary industry, and have achieved remarkable results in environmental pollution control. Yet their UCLU remains suboptimal in terms of intensity: driven by tourism-related spatial demands and landscape-oriented planning priorities, UCL in these cities tends to be spatially fragmented and characterized by low floor-area ratios.

In sharp contrast to the above-mentioned cities, Baiyin, Jincheng, and Songyuan are the cities with the weakest sustainable development capabilities of UCL in the L-L group. Baiyin is an important base for the non-ferrous metal industry in China, Jincheng is a typical coal resource-based city, and Songyuan is a mining city dominated by oil. It is evident that these three cities have one thing in common: they are all resource-based cities that initially relied on abundant natural resources to rapidly promote urban development. However, this over-reliance on natural resources led to disorderly expansion of their UCL, disrupting the original balance of the land and resulting in inefficient UCL circulation, characterized by high consumption and low output. Moreover, the high-energy-consumption and high-emission model associated with resource development and utilization has caused serious environmental pollution, hindering the low-carbon and sustainable development of UCL [23]. This pattern applies to most cities in the L-L group.

Based on these classification results and drawing on the multiobjective decision-making approach of Yang et al. [56], cities should consider both economic development and emission-reduction objectives when selecting measures suited to local resources and development needs. Policy priorities should also reflect regional functional roles and local resource conditions [57,58]. H-L cities could prioritize energy-saving upgrades, cleaner energy substitution, and industrial upgrading to improve low-carbon performance while maintaining economic output and employment and accounting for transition costs. L-H cities should strengthen the consolidation and redevelopment of underutilized land while preserving their ecological and low-carbon advantages, avoiding additional energy demand from pursuing greater development intensity alone. L-L cities need to coordinate industrial transformation with improvements in existing land use, sequencing measures according to fiscal capacity, industrial conditions, and employment needs. Land management and low-carbon development practices in H-H cities may provide useful references, although their application requires adaptation to local conditions. These measures should be prioritized according to local development objectives, balancing socioeconomic benefits, emission reductions, and implementation costs within land, planning, and fiscal constraints.

sec.title: 4.3. Variations in UCLUE Across City Size Classes
sec.p: For both UCLUE-IN and UCLUE-LC, a consistent trend emerges across city-size categories: megacities > huge cities > large cities > medium-sized cities > small cities. This gradient aligns with previous research findings [2], suggesting that cities with larger populations tend to have higher average UCLUE values. Several interconnected factors may help explain the observed disparities. Firstly, cities with larger populations typically possess greater institutional resources to implement sophisticated land use planning, revitalize underutilized land, and enforce strict development controls [16]. This capacity enables them to achieve higher output per land unit while maintaining relatively lower carbon emission intensity, whereas smaller cities often lack the technical and institutional capacity for such refined management. Secondly, as Wei et al. [59] demonstrated, the core-to-periphery pattern of UCL expansion can generate structural misalignment between socioeconomic development and UCLU. Compared to larger cities, smaller cities are more prone to such expansion issues, resulting in a disconnection between UCLU and the city’s development level, and a consequent lack of UCL sustainable development capacity [60]. Thirdly, larger cities benefit from pronounced suction effects, attracting skilled talent, investment, and fiscal resources from surrounding areas [48]. These resources may support more diversified economies with higher shares of services and knowledge-intensive industries that generate greater output per land unit with lower emissions. In contrast, smaller cities often remain dependent on resource extraction or traditional manufacturing—sectors that are both land-extensive and carbon-intensive, which may contribute to the observed UCLUE gap. These findings imply the need for differentiated policy strategies. For smaller cities, priority should be strengthening planning capacity and controlling disorderly expansion. For larger cities, the focus should be deepening low-carbon transformation while maintaining intensive use advantages.

sec.title: 4.4. Limitations and Future Prospects
sec.p: Several limitations of this study should be noted. Given data scarcity at the city level and differences in statistical standards, this study primarily relies on traditional economic and social indicators. GDP-based energy allocation and linear interpolation may introduce measurement uncertainty. Future research should adopt more comprehensive and precise measurement indicators as data availability improves. Additionally, future research should prioritize identifying the driving factors of sustainable land-use development within this two-stage framework.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p:
This study employed a two-stage super-SBM model to measure the UCLUE of 268 Chinese cities during 2001–2021 from the perspectives of intensification and low-carbon. The main findings are as follows:(1)
The average efficiency from the intensification perspective remains relatively low across the sample cities, showing a fluctuating trend characterized by an initial rise, a subsequent decline, and a final rebound. Pronounced regional disparities exist in this intensification dimension, with the eastern, western, and central regions ranking from highest to lowest, respectively. Improving the use of existing construction land therefore remains a priority, particularly in cities with relatively low intensification efficiency. Redevelopment should be matched to local demand and financial capacity to avoid costly projects that create additional underused space.(2)
The average efficiency from the low-carbon perspective follows a U-shaped trajectory, with the eastern region performing best, followed by the western region, while the central region ranks lowest. The recovery in UCLUE-LC indicates progress in low-carbon land use, although regional disparities persist. Further improvements in relatively inefficient cities call for energy-saving upgrades and industrial restructuring, with a phased approach that balances emission reductions, transition costs, and employment needs.(3)
Under the mean-based classification, the largest proportion of the 268 sample cities falls into the Low–Low development mode, reaching 54.48%, while the shares of High–High, High–Low, and Low–High modes are lower at 19.78%, 12.31%, and 13.43%, respectively. This indicates that relatively few cities perform above the national averages in both dimensions, whereas more than half fall below both averages. Among these cities, Shenzhen, Shanghai, and Nanjing demonstrate the strongest sustainable development capabilities, whereas Baiyin, Jincheng, and Songyuan exhibit the weakest. Furthermore, cities with larger populations generally display stronger land use sustainability. Future policy efforts should focus on improving planning capacity and resource allocation in small and medium-sized cities, while larger cities should advance low-carbon development alongside intensive land use. Implementation should account for local fiscal capacity and industrial conditions.
